High Blood Pressure and Diabetes · Lesson 5

Know Your Numbers

A flipchart for Care Group meetings. Show the picture side to the group. Turn to the text side to read the story, the questions and the messages.

  • Next and Back, or a swipe, turn the page.
  • Tap a picture to make it fill the screen.

Lesson 5 at a glance

90 minutes. Bring the attendance registers, this flipchart, ten number cards, blank record cards and pens. The Activity Leader brings a rope or chalk. Participants bring their clinic cards.

Before the pictures

Game: Clap on Seven. The group counts aloud round the circle. The person who reaches seven claps and does not say the number. At fourteen, clap twice. A mistake starts the count again.

Recall Lesson 4. In diabetes, too much sugar stays in the blood. The signs are great thirst, passing urine often and tiredness. Many people have no signs. High sugar harms the eyes, the heart, the kidneys, the nerves and the feet.

Commitments. Ask: “What was your commitment at the last lesson? Have you been able to keep it?”

After the pictures

Which Side of the Line? Lay a rope on the ground. One side is “at the aim”. The other side is “too high”. Read each number card aloud. Participants walk to the side they think is right.

  • Blood pressure, at the aim: 118/76, 136/84, 128/88.
  • Blood pressure, too high: 150/95 (both numbers), 145/85 (top number), 135/95 (bottom number).
  • Sugar before food, at the aim: 5.8 and 6.9. Too high: 11 and 14.

Then, in pairs, each person finds her last blood pressure reading on her own clinic card. Nobody has to read her numbers aloud. Give a blank record card to anyone who has no card.

Practise together, twice: “Please, what are my numbers today? What is my aim?”

Discuss barriers. Ask: “Is there anything that might prevent you from asking for your numbers and keeping your card?”

Request commitments. Ask: “Based on what you have heard today, what commitment will you make?” Each person chooses. Do not press anyone who is not ready.

Picture 5.1Story: Two Numbers on Naa’s Card

Picture 5.1 · text sideStory: Two Numbers on Naa’s Card

Read the story aloud.

Auntie Naa and Uncle Kofi go to the mission hospital together. The nurse checks Naa’s blood pressure. She says, “Today your pressure is 150 over 95.” Naa is confused. “Two numbers? Which one is my BP?”

The nurse checks Kofi’s sugar with a drop of blood. “Your sugar is 11.” Kofi asks, “Eleven. Is that good or bad? All these years, nobody told me.”

The nurse smiles. “Sit down, both of you. I will write your numbers on your cards. Then I will show you what they mean, and what numbers we are aiming for.”

Ask the group.

  • What numbers did the nurse tell Naa and Kofi?
  • Do you know your own numbers? Who told you?
  • Where do you keep your clinic card?

Encourage discussion. Do not correct “wrong” answers. Let everyone give an opinion. This page is for discussion, not for teaching.

Say “Let us compare your ideas with the messages on the following pages.”

Picture 5.2The Two Blood Pressure Numbers

Picture 5.2 · text sideThe Two Blood Pressure Numbers

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

Blood pressure has two numbers.

  • The top number is the push when the heart beats.
  • The bottom number is the push when the heart rests between beats.
  • We say them together, for example “150 over 95”. Both numbers matter.
B

For most adults, the aim is below 140 over 90.

  • If the top number is 140 or more, or the bottom number is 90 or more, the pressure is high.
  • Some people need a lower aim, for example people who also have diabetes or kidney problems. Ask your health worker, “What is my aim?”
C

Sit and rest before the check. Ask for your numbers.

  • Sit quietly for five minutes before the check. Do not talk during the check.
  • Ask, “Please, what are my numbers today?” Ask the health worker to write them on your card.
  • One reading can be high because you hurried or you are worried. What matters is the numbers over many visits.

Ask the group.

  • Naa’s pressure was 150 over 95. Is it at the aim? Which number is too high?
  • What will you ask the health worker at your next visit?
Additional information for the facilitator

Answer. Both of Naa’s numbers are too high: 150 is above 140, and 95 is above 90.

Sources. The World Health Organization states that high blood pressure is diagnosed when, on two different days, the top number is 140 or more, the bottom number is 90 or more, or both. It gives an aim of below 140 over 90 for most people, and below 130 over 80 for people who also have heart disease, a past stroke, diabetes, kidney disease or a high risk of heart disease. The health worker sets each person’s aim.

A good check. The person sits with the back supported and both feet on the floor, the arm rests on a table, and the person has not smoked, drunk coffee or hurried in the last half hour.

People who do not read numbers. Ask them to learn the two aims by ear: “below 140 over 90” and “sugar 7 or below”. A family member can read the card with them.

Picture 5.3The Sugar Number and Your Card

Picture 5.3 · text sideThe Sugar Number and Your Card

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

For sugar checked before food in the morning, the aim is 7 or below.

  • The health worker checks sugar with a small drop of blood.
  • Kofi’s sugar was 11. That is too high.
  • Sugar below 4 is too low. Lesson 21 explains what to do.
  • Ask your health worker, “What is my aim?”
B

Keep your card safe. Bring it to every visit.

  • The card shows whether your numbers are coming down.
  • Keep it with your health insurance card.
C

Share your numbers with your family.

  • Family members can help you to read and remember your numbers.
  • When the numbers come down and stay down, the Four Helpers are working.

Ask the group.

  • Where will you keep your card?
  • Who at home will you show your numbers to?
Additional information for the facilitator

Sugar numbers. In Ghana, blood sugar is reported in millimoles per litre (mmol/L). A value of 7.0 or more before food is used to diagnose diabetes, and 7 or below before food is a common aim for people on treatment, for example in the clinical guidelines of Médecins Sans Frontières. After a meal the number is higher. The health worker sets each person’s aim.

The three-month test. Some facilities, including those in Value-Based Care, also do a blood test called HbA1c. It shows the average sugar over about three months. A common aim is about 7 percent.

Checking at home. Lesson 20 covers checking blood pressure and sugar between clinic visits.
